## Interpretation

Troponins are released in response to myocardial injury regardless of cause. Ischemia is the most common cause of cardiac muscle damage, and the initial assays were developed as a marker to detect the presence of myocardial ischemia; however, elevation in troponin levels can occur in myriad conditions other than ischemic damage.

### Troponin release in cardiac injury

It is proposed that there is a small cytosolic pool and a larger muscular pool of troponins. During cardiac injury, depending on the severity, troponins are released from both pools. An initial small elevation occurs when troponins are released from the cytosolic pool, when troponin molecules in the cytosol of cardiac muscle diffuse across the sarcolemma into the surrounding lymphatics and blood vessels, becoming detectable in blood. If the injury persists and necrosis progresses, further troponins are released from the muscular pool. [[5](javascript:void(0);), [6](javascript:void(0);)]

### Pattern of rise and fall

Cardiac troponin levels begin to rise within 2-3 h of myocardial injury. After a myocardial infarction (MI), cTnI levels can remain elevated for 7-10 days, while cTnT levels may remain high for up to 14 days. hs-cTn assays can detect much lower troponin levels, allowing for earlier identification of MI, as soon as 90 min after the event. Monitoring the rise and fall of troponin levels helps distinguish acute coronary syndrome from other conditions that can cause troponin elevation. To improve diagnostic accuracy, troponin testing is typically repeated 1-3 h after the initial sample when high-sensitivity assays (or 3-6 h for sensitive assays) are used. [[2](javascript:void(0);)]

Modern assays have increased the sensitivity of point-of-care troponin testing in patients who present initially to the emergency department with symptoms suggestive of ischemia and myocardial damage. Most current guidelines recommend rechecking troponins 6-12 h after the initial assessment and up to 24 h after symptom onset. [[7](javascript:void(0);), [8](javascript:void(0);)]  In patients in whom subendocardial non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is highly suspected, the troponin levels may be re-evaluated earlier, at 3-4 h, as the markers may be detectable sooner. [[9](javascript:void(0);), [10](javascript:void(0);), [11](javascript:void(0);)]

In populations with NSTEMI and type 2 MI, females tend to present higher troponin/cutoff ratios than males, across both cTnI and cTnT. [[12](javascript:void(0);)]

### Troponin T and troponin I

Troponin T and troponin I are different molecules with different roles. While an elevation of either specifies myocardial damage, their absolute values differ. One standardized assay exists for troponin T, while multiple assays are available for troponin I; each has a different cutoff value as these assays target distinct epitopes.

Clinicians need to be aware of the abnormal reference range for the assays used in their practice and that absolute values from different assays do not correlate.

### Causes of troponin elevation other than myocardial infarction

Causes of troponin elevation other than MI include the following:

* [Myocarditis](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/156330-overview)
* Pericarditis
* Cardiac contusion/trauma
* [Aortic Dissection](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/2062452-overview)
* Endocarditis
* Cardiac surgery
* [Pulmonary Embolism](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/300901-overview)
* Stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic)
* [Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1344081-overview) (CPR)
* [Defibrillation](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/80564-overview)
* Chronic severe [Heart Failure](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/163062-overview)
* Cardiac arrhythmias (tachyarrhythmias, bradyarrhythmias, heart blocks)
* Sepsis
* [Renal failure](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/243492-overview)
* [Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/152913-overview)
* [Takotsubo cardiomyopathy](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1513631-overview)
* Burns
* Extreme exertion
* Post-cardiac surgery
* Infiltrative diseases such as [Amyloidosis](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/335414-overview)
* Medications and toxins such as doxorubicin, trastuzumab, and snake venom
* Transplant vasculopathy
* Critical illness
* Trauma [[2](javascript:void(0);)]

Elevated troponin levels should always be evaluated in a clinical context. While the incidence of elevated troponin levels in the general population is low and is generally associated with an underlying cardiac structural abnormality, any level of troponin elevation is associated with a worse prognosis in age- and disease-matched cohorts. This is especially true in critically ill patients with a diagnosis other than acute coronary syndrome, in whom elevated troponin levels have been shown to be associated with increased mortality. [[13](javascript:void(0);), [14](javascript:void(0);), [15](javascript:void(0);), [16](javascript:void(0);)]

There are various causes of troponin level elevation in the absence of coronary artery disease, as discussed below.

*Damage due to relative myocardial ischemia (type 2 myocardial infarction) from a supply-demand mismatch*

The troponin level may be elevated in the setting of a demand for an increased cardiac output and relatively inadequate myocardial blood flow. This can occur in sepsis, [[14](javascript:void(0);)]  septic shock, systemic inflammatory response system, hypotensive shock, hypovolemic shock, [[17](javascript:void(0);)]  cardiac arrhythmias (e.g., supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rate, tachyarrhythmias). [[18](javascript:void(0);), [19](javascript:void(0);)]  In patients with acute exacerbation of congestive heart failure due to etiologies even other than MI, troponin levels may be elevated because of the inability of the weak heart to maintain appropriate coronary perfusion.

Tachycardia from any etiology increases the cardiac oxygen demand and, owing to reduced diastolic filling time, reduces coronary perfusion. This relative supply demand mismatch can cause myocardial damage to some extent, increasing the troponin level.

In the setting of sepsis, septic shock, and acidosis, in addition to the increased myocardial oxygen demand, a relative myocardial depression contributes to demand ischemia.

Elevation in cardiac troponin levels has been noted in the setting of aortic valve disease. Individuals with aortic stenosis often have increased left ventricular thickness, and this increased muscle mass may contribute to demand-based subendocardial ischemia. [[20](javascript:void(0);)]  This also holds true for individuals with left ventricular hypertrophy. [[21](javascript:void(0);)]

Hypertensive emergency, coronary vasculitis, and aortic dissection may also cause an elevated troponin level due to type 2 MI.

*Elevated troponin levels caused by direct cardiac damage from agents other than ischemia*

Cardiac contusion due to blunt chest wall trauma can raise troponin levels stemming from direct injury to the ventricular muscle fibers. The combination of electrocardiography (ECG) and troponins has a high negative predictive value in diagnosing significant blunt cardiac injury, and, in the absence of other compelling reasons for hospitalization, these patients can be safely discharged. [[22](javascript:void(0);)]

Myocarditis from any etiology (e.g., viral, fungal, mycobacterial, bacterial) may elevate troponin levels owing to direct injury to the ventricular myocyte. [[23](javascript:void(0);)]  This causes membranous damage, myocyte necrosis, and release of troponin from the injured or necrosed myocytes. [[24](javascript:void(0);)]  Similarly, troponin levels may be elevated in the absence of ischemia in acute pericarditis due to ventricular myocyte injury. [[25](javascript:void(0);)]

Patients who receive CPR or external defibrillation [[26](javascript:void(0);)]  or shocks from an implantable cardioverter defibrillator may also have elevated troponin levels due to ventricular muscle damage.

Medications and chemicals that are directly cardiotoxic may also elevate troponin levels. Such agents include chemotherapeutic drugs such as cyclophosphamide, anthracyclines, and bevacizumab and chemicals such as carbon monoxide. Studies in patients receiving chemotherapeutic agents with known cardiotoxicity have shown that those who develop elevated troponin levels in the absence of ischemia are at an increased future risk of developing left ventricular failure and cardiomyopathy. [[27](javascript:void(0);)]

Infiltrative disorders such as amyloidosis may also cause elevated troponin levels.

Individuals who develop rhabdomyolysis with cardiac involvement may also have elevated troponin levels.

*Multiple factors*

Troponin elevation in stroke

Both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke have been associated with elevated troponin levels and ECG changes, although the degree of elevation is typically much lesser than that seen with acute MI. The exact etiology of this remains unclear, but autonomic dysfunction following stroke with an imbalance in the sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow to the heart may be a possible explanation.

In the setting of stroke, sympathetic input to the heart increases and catecholamines surge, which can affect the cardiac myocyte and increase troponin levels. Levels of other cardiac markers are often normal in this setting. In patients with stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage, elevated troponin levels have been associated with poor cardiac and neurological prognosis. [[28](javascript:void(0);)]

Peripartum cardiomyopathy and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy have also been associated with elevated troponin levels.

Troponin elevation with pulmonary disease

The presence of significant pulmonary disease strains the right ventricle by increasing the right ventricular afterload. This can result from acute pulmonary embolism and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in the setting of pulmonary hypertension.

Increased troponin levels may be seen with a large pulmonary embolism, presumably owing to increased right heart strain. [[29](javascript:void(0);)]  Elevated troponin levels in the setting of acute pulmonary embolism portends a worse prognosis than in patients without elevated troponin levels. [[30](javascript:void(0);)]

Similarly, troponin levels may be elevated in the setting of acute exacerbation of COPD and associated with increased in-hospital mortality. [[31](javascript:void(0);)]

Troponin elevation with renal disease

The evaluation of elevated troponin levels in patients with chronic kidney disease presents many challenges. In many asymptomatic patients with kidney disease, especially those on hemodialysis, troponin levels may be elevated. [[32](javascript:void(0);)]

In the absence of other clinical features of ischemia, elevated troponins alone may not be reliable and may be falsely positive, leading to unnecessary investigations. This is further confounded by the fact that patients with renal insufficiency are at an increased risk for silent ischemia and that cardiovascular diseases continue to be the leading cause of mortality in patients with kidney diseases.

Nonetheless, even asymptomatically elevated troponin levels are associated with a worse long-term prognosis in patients with chronic kidney disease. [[33](javascript:void(0);)]

In many cases, troponin T is more elevated than troponin I in patients with chronic kidney disease, even at baseline. [[32](javascript:void(0);), [33](javascript:void(0);)]  Although the exact reason for this is unknown, it has been postulated to result from a higher unbound cytosolic pool of troponin T, leading to early release and a higher molecular weight of troponin T (resulting in its delayed clearance from the kidneys). [[34](javascript:void(0);)]

## Collection and Panels

The troponin sample assay relies on serum levels of troponin. The sample collected is whole blood through venipuncture. No special patient preparation is needed, and fasting is not required. Blood for the test can be drawn at any time of the day.

The tubes in which the sample is collected are different for troponin T and troponin I, and the clinician should refer to the package insert for requirements. Generally, troponin T requires sample collection in heparinized test tubes (green top), while EDTA (purple top) or heparinized tubes are used for troponin I. [[35](javascript:void(0);), [36](javascript:void(0);)]  Most specimens require centrifugation prior to running the test in order to separate the serum from the cellular components.

### Sample storage

The clinician should refer to the assay's package insert for instructions. In general, for troponin T, the blood sample should not be frozen or refrigerated immediately, and it can be stored at room temperature for up to 8 h for analyses. [[35](javascript:void(0);)]

### Laboratory turnaround time

Currently, the consensus is that the turnaround time for troponin measurement in the setting of chest pain should be 60 min, and individual laboratories should strive to achieve this. [[37](javascript:void(0);)]

## Background

The skeletal and cardiac muscle troponin T and troponin I are immunologically distinct entities. [[5](javascript:void(0);)]  Separate sets of genes code for these proteins. Thus, the cardiac troponin assays, which rely on antigen antibody interaction, are specific for cardiac troponins and can be used to differentiate between the skeletal and cardiac troponins.

Cardiac troponin levels do not rise in the presence of skeletal damage without cardiac myocyte damage. However, this is not the case for creatine kinase MB, which — being present to some extent in skeletal muscle and several other tissues such as the intestines, tongue, diaphragm, uterus, and prostate — may be elevated upon injury to these tissues, potentially resulting in false-positive results. [[38](javascript:void(0);)]  Because of this, troponin testing is superior to creatine kinase MB testing.

*Ischemic heart disease*

Ischemic heart disease is a leading cause of death worldwide. Much advancement in early diagnosis and management of patients presenting with varying manifestations of ischemic heart disease has been made.

ECG was one of the earliest diagnostic modalities introduced to evaluate ischemic injury to the heart. Despite its usefulness, ECG continues to be nonsensitive in diagnosing ischemic cardiac events as ECG findings are normal in many patients with ischemic injury.

The introduction of various markers of cardiac injury, such as creatinine kinase MB, troponins, and myoglobins, has revolutionized the diagnosis of myocardial injury. The cardiac troponins, by virtue of being the most sensitive and specific, have become the preferred biomarker for evaluating patients with suspected MI. [[39](javascript:void(0);), [40](javascript:void(0);), [8](javascript:void(0);)]

hs-cTn assays are the global standard for diagnosing myocardial injury, offering rapid, precise measurements at very low concentrations. The 99th percentile upper reference limit (sex-specific) defines myocardial injury. [[41](javascript:void(0);)]

### Indications/Applications

Troponin values should be evaluated upon clinical suspicion of MI. This test aids in evaluating patients with suspected acute coronary ischemic syndromes. In addition to improving the diagnosis of acute ischemic events, cardiac troponins are valuable for risk stratification in patients with unstable angina and pulmonary embolism. [[2](javascript:void(0);)]

Elevated troponin T levels do not always indicate myocardial ischemia. Nonischemic causes include cardiac trauma (e.g., contusion, cardioversion, defibrillation), heart failure, hypertension, hypotension, pulmonary embolism, renal failure, and myocarditis. [[2](javascript:void(0);)]

*Detection of myocardial infarction*

Per the 2007 guidelines of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), the term "acute MI" should be used when there is evidence of myocardial necrosis in a clinical setting consistent with myocardial ischemia. One of the criteria is the detection of rising and falling cardiac biomarker levels, with at least one value above the 99th percentile of the upper reference limit. The preferred marker for the diagnosis of MI in this setting is troponin. [[40](javascript:void(0);)]  The Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction and major cardiovascular guidelines (ACC/AHA/European Society of Cardiology) mandate the use of hs-cTn assays for the detection of myocardial necrosis, with at least one value above the sex-specific 99th percentile upper reference limit and a characteristic rise and/or fall in the context of ischemic symptoms. [[41](javascript:void(0);)]  This is the single most important use of troponins in clinical medicine. Troponins are specific to cardiac muscle, rise fairly early in cardiac injury, and stay elevated longer than some of the other cardiac biomarkers such as creatine kinase-MB and myoglobin. Normal serial troponin values effectively rule out acute myocardial ischemia.

*Determining infarct size*

Peak troponin values can provide an estimate of the infarct size and the severity of myocardial damage. These values are more sensitive in the setting of transmural infarction (ST-segment–elevation MI [STEMI]) than in subendocardial infarctions (e.g., NSTEMI). [[42](javascript:void(0);), [43](javascript:void(0);)]  This correlation holds true for both troponin T [[44](javascript:void(0);), [42](javascript:void(0);)]  and troponin I [[45](javascript:void(0);)]  (peak or values at 72-96 h). Higher values generally correlate with a larger infarct.

*Significance of the degree of troponin elevation*

The degree of troponin elevation correlates well with both the 30-day mortality and long-term mortality. Various clinical trials have evaluated the degree of elevation of both troponin I and troponin T and found that higher elevations at presentation and peak are associated with worse long-term outcomes. The absolute values have been used to guide treatment decisions and to identify patients who are at an increased risk for death. [[46](javascript:void(0);), [47](javascript:void(0);), [48](javascript:void(0);), [49](javascript:void(0);)]

*Prognostic value of the timing of elevation*

Patients who present with elevated troponin levels at baseline tend to have worse outcomes than those in whom troponin levels are elevated at 8 h. Outcomes are best in patients in whom troponin levels never increase. [[50](javascript:void(0);)]

In both STEMI and NSTEMI, elevated troponin T and troponin I levels at presentation are associated with a worse prognosis in terms of both short-term and long-term mortality.

Improved diagnostic pathways using hs-cTn have shortened emergency department stays and reduced unnecessary admissions while maintaining safety. [[51](javascript:void(0);)]

COVID 19–associated myocardial injury occurs in hospitalized patients and correlates with increased mortality and intensive care unit admissions. Scoping and cohort reviews consistently show that even modest hs-cTn elevations predict worse outcomes (e.g., death, need for mechanical ventilation) in patients with COVID 19. [[52](javascript:void(0);)]

*How often to perform troponin testing and the need for serial testing*

In patients with MI, there is a lag before troponin elevations can be detected. Thus, the markers should be serially monitored upon suspicion for acute coronary syndrome. [[50](javascript:void(0);)]  The 2025 AHA/ACC/ASE/CHEST/SAEM/SCCT/SCMR guidelines for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes strongly recommend the use of hs-cTN assays as the preferred standard for diagnosing acute MI. Serial measurements of troponin levels (e.g., at 0, 1, 2, or 3 h) are often used to assess for changes indicative of MI, especially in patients with elevated levels at presentation.

### Considerations

Some of the analytical interfering factors that may lead to falsely elevated troponin levels include the following [[8](javascript:void(0);), [53](javascript:void(0);), [54](javascript:void(0);), [55](javascript:void(0);)] :

* Incompletely clotted specimen (e.g., in patients with coagulopathy or on anticoagulant therapy) [[56](javascript:void(0);)]
* Heterophile antibodies, human anti-animal antibodies [[57](javascript:void(0);)]
* Rheumatoid factor [[58](javascript:void(0);), [59](javascript:void(0);)]  and autoantibodies
* Elevated bilirubin levels [[60](javascript:void(0);)]
* Immunocomplex formation [[61](javascript:void(0);)]
* Markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase levels [[62](javascript:void(0);)]
* Analyzer malfunction [[63](javascript:void(0);)]
